newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia '98 draft budget assumes two pct growth.
newsitem.headline: Russia '98 draft budget assumes two pct growth.

text.p: Russia's 1998 draft budget assumes the economy will grow by two percent next year, the deputy head of President Boris Yeltsin's administration said on Friday.
This would make 1998 the first year of recovery for Russia since economic reforms began. But Alexander Livshits said the budget would be Russia's first realistic one.
"The figures are like this -- two percent real growth and annual inflation of five to seven percent," Alexander Livshits told a news conference. "The figures are realistic enough."
Russia's gross domestic product fell by 0.2 percent in the first seven months of 1997, compared to the same period last year.
Ministers now say GDP will be flat this year, although there are signs of growth. They had previously hoped that 1997 would be the first year of recovery.
The 1997 budget foresees 11.8 percent annual inflation, but First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais has said recently the rate will be a little higher.
The finance ministry said the 1998 draft budget provides for revenues of 12.37 percent of GDP and expenditure of 17.20 percent.
The government now expects revenues of 13.00 percent of GDP in 1997, and expenditure of 18.35 percent.
"The government is undoubtedly able to raise such money," Livshits said.
The government failed to fulfil the 1996 budget and has had to sequester or cut the 1997 budget by 108 trillion roubles ($18.58 billion) due to low tax collection.
Livshits, who was finance minister until March this year, said proceeds from privatisation, would be less than in 1997.
"We do not expect in 1998 the same revenues from privatisation as we had this year," he said. "They will be less, and significantly less."
The government has raised about seven trillion roubles from privatisation so far this year.
Livshits said Yeltsin had ordered the government to increase spending on military reforms, health and education next year.
He said the draft budget provided for a foreign borrowing ceiling of 30 trillion roubles.
Previously the government said it planned to attract $9.6 billion from foreign markets and international lending agencies in 1998, including $3 billion from Eurobonds.

Livshits said Russia planned to extend 265 billion roubles more of tied credits -- loans which must be spent only on buying goods from companies of the creditor-country -- to other countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States in 1998.
The government will finalise the draft budget on August 21, he said. By law it must be passed to the State Duma lower house of parliament no later than August 25. ($ = 5,813 roubles)
